title: rfaR: Reservoir Frequency Analysis in R
text:
Preface
rfaR is an R implementation of the RMC Reservoir Frequency Analysis (RMC-RFA) methodology. This package produces hydrologic hazard curves with uncertainty bounds by combining deterministic Modified Puls flood routing with a nested Monte Carlo framework.
This manual complements the function reference site generated by pkgdown. The function reference site documents individual functions. This manual explains the methodology and provides instructions to set up an rfaR analysis.






Warning



rfaR is under active development. Its application programming interface (API) may change without notice.



How to cite


To cite rfaR:

  McGraw D, Verdin A, Smith C (2026). _rfaR: RMC Reservoir Frequency
  Analysis in R_. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Risk Management Center,
  Lakewood, CO. <https://github.com/USACE-RMC/rfaR>.

A BibTeX entry for LaTeX users is

  @Manual{,
    title = {rfaR: RMC Reservoir Frequency Analysis in R},
    author = {Daniel McGraw and Andrew Verdin and C. Haden Smith},
    organization = {U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Risk Management Center},
    address = {Lakewood, CO},
    year = {2026},
    version = {0.9.0},
    url = {https://github.com/USACE-RMC/rfaR},
  }

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Purpose
rfaR is an R implementation of the Risk Management Center’s Reservoir Frequency Analysis software (RMC-RFA). This package produces hydrologic hazard curves with uncertainty bounds by combining deterministic flood routing with a nested Monte Carlo framework. Hydrologic hazard analyses support risk assessments in accordance with the USACE Dam & Levee Safety Program (DLS).
The intended use of rfaR is to generate hydrologic hazard curves/loading curves1, supporting risk analyses for dams and levees. The development of rfaR was primarily to conduct hazard analyses using GEV inflow volume-frequency parameters, developed from partial duration series in arid locations (RMC-RFA only supports LPIII parameters). Additional package development incorporates analysis at levees (no reservoir routing), transforming sampled unregulated inflow values to regulated inflow values, and a stage-based probabilistic bounding of hydrologic hazard curves.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 rfaR Analysis Summary
rfaR combines deterministic flood routing (Modified Puls) with a nested, two-loop Monte Carlo framework. The nested framework handles both natural variability and knowledge uncertainty:

Natural variability — simulated in the inner loop as a realization. Each realization represents 10,000 indiviual flood events with randomly sampled starting stages, hydrograph shapes, and inflow volumes (from an associated inflow-frequency distribution).
Knowledge uncertainty (epistemic uncertainty) — simulated in the outer loop, by sampling different inflow-frequency parameter sets (from LP3 or GEV flood frequency distributions, informed by RMC-BestFit’s MCMC output).

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 Scope and Limitations
rfaR implements the core RMC-RFA methodology into R, a populatr open-source statisical language. rfaR is intended to serve as a bridge between the current release of RMC-RFA and the planned second version of RMC-RFA. As of November 2026, users cannot import an existing RMC-RFA model or input file directly into rfaR; users must prepare the required inputs separately.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 User Manual Outline

Installation — System requirements and instructions for installing and loading rfaR.
Set Up an rfaR Analysis — Prepare a new rfaR analysis, including project organization and input-data preparation.
Methodology — Statistical and hydrologic methods underlying the two-loop simulation framework.
Workflow — Detailed guidance for using rfa_simulate(), defining input options and simulation settings, and processing outputs.
Validation — Compare rfaR results with RMC-RFA and HEC-HMS benchmark results.
Function Reference — Reference documentation for rfaR functions and their arguments.
References

For function-level documentation, also see the pkgdown reference site.

title: 1  Introduction
text: In risk analysis, the hazard is the risk source where potential consequences relate to harm (Aven et al., n.d.). In the context of dam and levee risk analyses, the source of risk is often defined using a reservoir stage-frequency relationship. The terms hydrologic loading, stage-frequency, and hydrologic hazard are used interchangeably to relate reservoir/river stages to annual exceedance probabilities (AEPs). These relationships are commonly presented as curves and are used as probabilistic loading conditions in dam and levee risk analyses.↩︎

title: 2  Installation
text:
2.1 System Requirements
rfaR is currently not available on the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN). The package source code is available from the USACE-RMC GitHub repository.

title: 2  Installation
text:
R version 4.1 or later
Internet access to reach the USACE-RMC/rfaR GitHub repository
Recommended: IDE geared towards science & engineering, such as RStudio RStudio or Positron

title: 2  Installation
text:
2.2 Install rfaR

2.2.1 Install with remotes (recommended)
Install the remotes package and then install rfaR from GitHub:
install.packages("remotes")

remotes::install_github(
  "USACE-RMC/rfaR",
  build_vignettes = FALSE
)


2.2.2 Install with devtools (developers and contributors)
Users who plan to modify the package source should clone the repository and work from a local copy of the project. After cloning the repository with Git or GitHub Desktop, open an R session or RStudio Project from the repository root directory.
Install devtools if it is not already available (requires Rtools):
install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("USACE-RMC/rfaR")
During active development, load the package source into the current R session without installing it:
devtools::load_all()
To install the local working copy of rfaR into your R library, run:
devtools::install()






Note



Cloning the repository does not make library(rfaR) available. To use the package, install it with devtools::install() or remotes::install_github(), or load the source for development with devtools::load_all().

title: 2  Installation
text:
2.3 Dependencies
Required package dependencies are declared in the rfaR DESCRIPTION file and are installed automatically during installation. Installing rfaR with remotes or devtools installs required R package dependencies as needed.
USACE users may encounter package download, installation, or compatibility issues because of network controls, repository-access restrictions, or locally managed R environments.
To report an installation or version-compatibility issue, open an issue in the rfaR GitHub repository. Include the R version, operating system, installation method, and complete error message when possible. Do not include Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI), credentials, access tokens, or other nonpublic system information in a GitHub issue.

title: 2  Installation
text:
2.4 Verify Installation
Load rfaR and confirm that the installed version and included example data are available:
# Load package
library(rfaR)
# Check package version
packageVersion("rfaR")
# Print some example data
head(jmd_wy1980_stage)
If these commands run without error, rfaR is installed and ready to use.

title: 3  Set Up an rfaR Analysis
text:
3.1 Create a Project Directory
This chapter provides a walkthrough example to set up, create, and execute an rfaR analysis.
Create a dedicated directory1 for each rfaR analysis. Store project inputs, scripts, and outputs in a location where you have write access, such as your user Documents directory. Do not create analyses in protected system directories, such as C:\Program Files.
The following example creates an rfaR-analysis directory in the current user’s home directory and creates subdirectories for input data, scripts, and outputs. The commands will create a folder structure to support a single rfaR analysis. Users can create the same file structure graphically using Windows Explorer.
The resulting directory structure is now:
crumbs: 3  Set Up an rfaR Analysis

title: 3  Set Up an rfaR Analysis
text:
# Set a base directory
# base_dir <- file.path("C:/path/to/your/project/")

# Define the project directory (replace path.expand("~") with base_dir)
project_dir <- file.path(path.expand("~"), "rfaR-analysis")

# Define project subdirectories
project_dirs <- c(
  project_dir,
  file.path(project_dir, "data"),
  file.path(project_dir, "data", "raw"),
  file.path(project_dir, "data", "processed"),
  file.path(project_dir, "output"),
  file.path(project_dir, "scripts")
)

# Create directories if they do not already exist
invisible(lapply(
  project_dirs,
  dir.create,
  recursive = TRUE,
  showWarnings = FALSE
))

rfaR-analysis/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   └── processed/
├── output/
└── scripts/

Store original source data in data/raw/.
Store cleaned, reformatted, or derived datasets in data/processed/.
Store analysis scripts in scripts/.
Store simulation results, figures, tables, and exported files in output/.

section: 3.2 Import Data from Existing RMC-RFA Projects using rfaScrape
text:
3.2 Import Data from Existing RMC-RFA Projects using rfaScrape
Direct integration between RMC-RFA SQLite project files and rfaR is under development. Until that capability is available, the recommended approach for extracting organized input data and analysis results from an existing RMC-RFA project is to use the rfaScrape package.
rfaScrape extracts data and results from RMC-RFA project files with the .rfa.sqlite extension and exports them to organized CSV directories. The package is intended to improve the organization, transfer, and reporting of RMC-RFA project data for use in downstream analyses. Future rfaR development is expected to incorporate functionality that supports more direct use of data from existing RMC-RFA projects.
Note that rfaScrape is not required to create required data fo rfaR analyses. Users may elect to create and organize data as they see fit.

3.2.1 R Project
Users working in RStudio may optionally create an RStudio Project in the rfaR-analysis directory. An RStudio Project helps maintain consistent working directory but is not required to run rfaR.


3.2.2 Positron
Positron organizes projects around directories and VS code-style workspaces. Users familiar with VS Code my prefer this working structure.

title: 3  Set Up an rfaR Analysis
text:
3.3 Load Input Data
rfaR analyses currently use input data stored in comma-separated values (CSV) files. Export or save the required input datasets as CSV files and store them in the project data/raw/ directory. This manual uses the base R function read.csv() for all examples. Users may instead use readr::read_csv() if they prefer the readr import workflow; however, the resulting data must meet the formatting requirements described in the following sections.
The example below imports a CSV file from the project input-data directory. Use head() to review the first rows of the imported dataset. Use str() to confirm the number of observations, variable names, and R data types.
# Define the path to an input CSV file
input_file <- file.path(
  project_dir,
  "data",
  "raw",
  "example_input.csv"
)

# Import the CSV file
input_data <- read.csv(input_file)

# Review the imported data
head(input_data)
str(input_data)
Users who are new to importing, cleaning, or restructuring data in R may find the following resources helpful:

Reading .csv files using read.csv() or readr::read_csv()
Data Import
Data Transform

title: 3  Set Up an rfaR Analysis
text:
3.4 Input Data
Example input data required formatting is included within this section. Updates to reflect on-going package development will be applied as completed.

3.4.1 Inflow Hydrographs
Inflow hydrographs define the shape2 of inflow events. Each hydrograph should represent a historical, synthetic, design, or other representative flood event. During a simulation, rfaR samples one of the provided hydrograph shapes and scales the peak to the sampled inflow-volume magnitude.
Use hydrograph_setup() to prepare one or more input hydrographs for use in rfa_simulate(). Input hydrographs can be imported or generated by the user in R.

3.4.1.1 Required Format
Each input hydrograph must be a data frame with the following columns in this order:








Column
Description
Required format




Ordinate
Sequential row or ordinate number.
Integer or numeric.


Date
Date associated with each inflow observation.
Character string in month/day/year format, such as "2/2/2099".


Time
Time associated with each inflow observation.
Character string in hour:minute format, such as "0:00" or "13:30".


Flow
Inflow discharge for each time step.
Numeric flow in cubic feet per second (cfs). Character values containing comma separators are also supported.



The hydrograph records must be in chronological order and use a regular time step. hydrograph_setup() determines the time step from the first two observations in each hydrograph.
The following example shows the format of an example hydrograph (jmd_hydro_pmf). Although the Ordinate column is retained in the input format for consistency with RMC-RFA exports, rfaR uses the Date, Time, and Flow columns to construct the simulation hydrograph.
  Ordinate     Date Time Flow
1        1 2/2/2099 0:00 1131
2        2 2/2/2099 1:00 1890
3        3 2/2/2099 2:00 2277
4        4 2/2/2099 3:00 1936
5        5 2/2/2099 4:00 1934
6        6 2/2/2099 5:00 1933


3.4.1.2 Import Hydrograph Data from CSV
Store hydrograph CSV files in the project data/raw/ directory. The following example imports three hydrographs and reviews the contents of the hydrograph data frames.
hydro_pmf <- read.csv(
  file.path(project_dir, "data", "raw", "hydro_pmf.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

hydro_jun1965 <- read.csv(
  file.path(project_dir, "data", "raw", "hydro_jun1965.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

hydro_may1955 <- read.csv(
  file.path(project_dir, "data", "raw", "hydro_may1955.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Review
head(hydro_pmf)
str(hydro_pmf)


3.4.1.3 Prepare Hydrographs for Simulation
Use hydrograph_setup() to format the imported hydrographs for simulation.
hydrographs <- hydrograph_setup(
  hydro_pmf,
  hydro_jun1965,
  hydro_may1955,
  critical_duration = 2, # Critical duration in DAYS
  routing_days = 10
)
The critical_duration argument specifies the inflow duration, in days, used to calculate the critical-duration inflow statistic for each hydrograph. The critical duration should align with the duration used for the inflow-volume frequency analysis. It must also correspond to a whole number of hydrograph time steps.
The routing_days argument specifies the desired total duration, in days, of each hydrograph used in routing. If a hydrograph is shorter than the specified routing duration, hydrograph_setup() extends the hydrograph by appending zero-flow time steps.


3.4.1.4 Hydrograph Sampling Weights
By default, rfaR assigns equal sampling probability to each supplied hydrograph. Use the optional weights argument to assign different relative sampling weights.
hydrographs <- hydrograph_setup(
  hydro_pmf,
  hydro_jun1965,
  hydro_may1955,
  critical_duration = 2,
  routing_days = 10,
  weights = c(3, 1, 1)
)
In this example, hydro_pmf has three times the relative sampling weight of each historical hydrograph. The supplied weights are normalized internally to produce sampling probabilities. Use attr to view the normalized probabilities.
attr(hydrographs, "probs")


3.4.1.5 Output
hydrograph_setup() returns a list of formatted hydrograph data frames. Each formatted hydrograph includes the following variables:







Variable
Description




datetime
Date-time value converted to POSIXct.


hour
Elapsed hours from the start of the hydrograph.


inflow
Inflow discharge in cfs.


hydrograph_num
Numeric identifier used during hydrograph sampling.



The list returned by hydrograph_setup() also contains attributes for each provided hydrograph. Attributes are named metadata pairs attached to any object to store extra information.







Attribute
Description




obs_vol
Critical-duration inflow statistic calculated from the observed hydrograph.


dt
Hydrograph time step in hours.


name
Name of the input hydrograph object.


probs
(List attribute) Normalized sampling probabilities



# Review the first formatted hydrograph
head(hydrographs[[1]])

# Review hydrograph attributes
attributes(hydrographs[[1]])

# Review hydrograph sampling probabilities
attr(hydrographs, "probs")

Note: hydrograph_setup() removes trailing rows with missing flow values, which can occur when CSV files are exported from spreadsheet software. Review the input data before analysis and correct missing or malformed values within the hydrograph record.




3.4.2 Bestfit Parameter Sets
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) Risk Management Center (RMC), in collaboration with the Engineer Research and Development Center (ERDC) Coastal and Hydraulics Laboratory (CHL), developed the Bayesian estimation and fitting software (RMC-BestFit) to enhance and expedite flood hazard assessments within the Flood Risk Management, Planning, and Dam and Levee Safety communities of practice.
The results of a volume-frequency analysis in BestFit result in a quantification of distribution parameter uncertainty. Posterior parameter sets are one of the various outs from BestFit that displays the parameter uncertainty. The BestFit user manual & technical reference recommend 10,000 parameter sets to ensure accurate 90% credible intervals.
bestfit_params contains 10,000 flood-frequency distribution parameter sets used to sample inflow magnitudes during an rfaR simulation. Each row represents one set of Bayesian estimated distribution parameters. Collectively, the parameter sets represent uncertainty in the fitted flood-frequency relationship. The included jmd_bf_parameter_sets example contains 10,000 Log-Pearson Type III (LP3) parameter sets.
Note that RMC-RFA conducts parameter sampling from bootstrapped volume-frequency curves, represented by the Effective Record Length (ERL) of the Bayesian volume-frequency estimates.

3.4.2.1 Required Format
Provide bestfit_params as a data frame. The first three columns must contain the distribution parameters in the order required by the selected distribution. All parameter fields must be numeric.








Distribution
Required parameter order
Description




LP3
mean_log, sd_log, skew_log
Mean, standard deviation, and skewness in log space.


GEV
location, scale, shape
Location, scale, and shape parameters of the generalized extreme value distribution.



The sampling functions use the first three columns by position. For that reason, place the three required parameter fields first, in the order shown above. An optional fourth log_likelihood column may be included. rfaR does not use this field during sampling.
The included LP3 example has the following structure:
head(jmd_bf_parameter_sets)
  mean_log    sd_log  skew_log log_likelihood
1 3.573019 0.3754496 0.5437323      -1093.040
2 3.560287 0.3599150 0.7516113      -1092.829
3 3.572810 0.3672706 0.7813260      -1092.882
4 3.508482 0.3586173 0.7270477      -1093.707
5 3.559233 0.3890737 0.4078201      -1093.874
6 3.514285 0.3907049 0.7473218      -1093.999
str(jmd_bf_parameter_sets)
'data.frame': 10000 obs. of 4 variables:
 $ mean_log      : num  3.57 3.56 3.57 3.51 3.56 ...
 $ sd_log        : num  0.375 0.360 0.367 0.359 0.389 ...
 $ skew_log      : num  0.544 0.752 0.781 0.727 0.408 ...
 $ log_likelihood: num  -1093 -1093 -1093 -1094 -1094 ...


3.4.2.2 Import Parameter Sets
Store parameter-set CSV files in the project data/raw/ directory. Import the file with read.csv() and preserve the original column order.
bestfit_params <- read.csv(
  file.path(project_dir, "data", "raw", "bestfit_parameter_sets.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

head(bestfit_params)
str(bestfit_params)
Before running a simulation, verify that the first three fields are numeric and are in the correct order for the selected distribution:
names(bestfit_params)[1:3]
str(bestfit_params[1:3])


3.4.2.3 Number of Parameter Sets
For an expected-only simulation, rfaR pairs each stratified sample with a different parameter set. Therefore, bestfit_params must contain at least NBins x EventsPerBin rows. The default settings in rfa_simulate() use Nbins = 50 and events_per_bin = 200, which require at least 10,000 parameter sets for an expected-only simulation.
required_parameter_sets <- 50 * 200
nrow(bestfit_params) >= required_parameter_sets
The following example uses the included 10,000 LP3 parameter sets with the default number of samples:
result <- rfa_simulate(
  sim_type = "expected",
  bestfit_params = jmd_bf_parameter_sets,
  dist = "LP3",
  stage_ts = jmd_wy1980_stage,
  seasonality = jmd_seasonality$relative_frequency,
  hydrographs = jmd_hydrographs,
  resmodel = jmd_resmodel,
  Nbins = 50,
  events_per_bin = 200
)


3.4.2.4 Distribution Selection
Set the dist argument in rfa_simulate() to match the parameterization of bestfit_params:
# LP3 parameter sets: mean_log, sd_log, skew_log
rfa_simulate(..., bestfit_params = bestfit_params, dist = "LP3")

# GEV parameter sets: location, scale, shape
rfa_simulate(..., bestfit_params = bestfit_params, dist = "GEV")
Do not use LP3 parameter sets with dist = "GEV", or GEV parameter sets with dist = "LP3". The parameter values may be numeric in both cases, but they have different meanings and are passed to different distribution functions.

Note: The parameter-set input represents uncertainty in the fitted frequency curve. It is not a table of observed flood events. Prepare observed inflow records, hydrograph shapes, and seasonal occurrence data separately.




3.4.3 Flood Seasonality
Flood seasonality defines the relative likelihood that a simulated flood event occurs in each calendar month. rfaR uses these probabilities to sample an event month for every simulated event. It then samples an antecedent reservoir stage from the observed stage record for the corresponding calendar month.
Provide flood seasonality to rfa_simulate() through the seasonality argument. In most cases, this input is the relative_frequency column from a monthly seasonality analysis.

3.4.3.1 Required Format
The seasonality argument must be a numeric vector with 12 values. The values must be ordered from January (1) through December (12). Each value represents the relative frequency of a flood occurring during that month. Values must be nonnegative, and at least one value must be greater than zero. The values should normally sum to 1.0. A monthly seasonality table may also include event counts and cumulative probabilities. rfaR uses only the vector of monthly relative frequencies. The included jmd_seasonality example has the following structure:
head(jmd_seasonality)
     month frequency relative_frequency cume_rel_frequency
1  January         0              0.000              0.000
2 February         0              0.000              0.000
3    March         0              0.000              0.000
4    April         1              0.018              0.018
5      May        14              0.246              0.263
6     June        17              0.298              0.561
In the example, the relative frequency is contained within jmd_seasonality$relative_frequency column. This shoudl be specified when calling rfa_simulate().
seasonality <- jmd_seasonality$relative_frequency

rfa_simulate(
  sim_type = "expected",
  bestfit_params = jmd_bf_parameter_sets,
  stage_ts = jmd_wy1980_stage,
  seasonality = seasonality,
  hydrographs = jmd_hydrographs,
  resmodel = jmd_resmodel
)
Again, note that the the minimum required input is a numeric vector of 12 values between 0 and 1, where each value represents the relative probability of flood occurrence for a calendar month from January through December. The values should sum to 1.


3.4.3.2 Import Flood Seasonality Data
Store seasonality input data in the project data/raw/ directory. The following example imports a monthly seasonality table from a CSV file:
seasonality_table <- read.csv(
  file.path(project_dir, "data", "raw", "flood_seasonality.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

head(seasonality_table)
str(seasonality_table)

# Extract the  monthly relative-frequency vector
seasonality <- seasonality_table$relative_frequency

# Check the relative-frequency sums to 1.0
stopifnot(length(seasonality) == 12)
stopifnot(all(seasonality >= 0))
stopifnot(sum(seasonality) > 0)

sum(seasonality)
If rounding causes the total to differ slightly from 1.0, normalize the vector before simulation:
seasonality <- seasonality / sum(seasonality)


3.4.3.3 Relationship to the Observed Stage Record
For each sampled event, rfaR samples a month using the seasonality relative-frequency. This month is used to randomly sample an antecedent reservoir stage from the observed stage time series during the sampled month. As a result, the observed stage time series must contain valid stage observations for every month with a nonzero seasonality probability.
For example, if June has a nonzero probability, the observed stage record must include valid June stage values. If the seasonality vector assigns nonzero probability to a month that has no corresponding stage observations, rfaR cannot draw an appropriate antecedent stage for events sampled in that month.


3.4.3.4 Seasonal Assumptions
The seasonality vector represents the assumed monthly distribution of flood event occurrence. Review the input before simulation to confirm that it is consistent with the flood-event definition, period of record, and inflow-volume frequency analysis used for the study. Months with a probability of zero are never sampled as event months.



3.4.4 Observed Stage Timeseries
The observed stage time series provides antecedent reservoir conditions used to randomly sample an initial reservoir stage for each simulated flood event. For each simulation, rfaR first samples a month using the flood-seasonality probabilities. It then samples an observed reservoir stage from the same calendar month in the stage record. This preserves the relationship between the seasonal timing of floods and observed reservoir stage. The user should provide a stage record that is representative of the reservoir operating conditions and period of analysis. The record should cover all months with a nonzero flood-seasonality probability. A longer record generally provides a larger sample of observed stages for each month.
Note that this differs from the method in RMC-RFA. In RFA, stage-duration curves for each month are generated and the initial reservoir stage is sampled from the selected month’s stage-duration. The difference between these methods is considered negligible and an analysis between the two methods is currently on-going.

3.4.4.1 Required Format
The stage time series should be provided as a data frame. The included jmd_wy1980_stage example contains four columns:








Column
Description
Required format




timestep
Sequential observation number.
Integer or numeric. This column is retained for traceability but is not used for monthly stage sampling.


date
Date associated with each stage observation.
Character string in month/day/year format, such as "10/1/1979".


time
Time associated with each stage observation.
Character string in hour:minute format, such as "0:00".


stage_ft
Observed reservoir stage.
Numeric stage elevation in feet. Use one consistent vertical datum throughout the analysis.



The date column is required because rfaR derives the calendar month from it. The stage column supplied to rfa_simulate() must be named stage. If the source data use a different name, such as stage_ft, rename that column before running the simulation. The example stage record is daily and begins on October 1, 1979:
head(jmd_wy1980_stage)
  timestep      date time stage_ft
1        1 10/1/1979 0:00  3790.68
2        2 10/2/1979 0:00  3790.64
3        3 10/3/1979 0:00  3790.60
4        4 10/4/1979 0:00  3790.60
5        5 10/5/1979 0:00  3790.61
6        6 10/6/1979 0:00  3790.61


3.4.4.2 Import and Prepare Stage Data
Store stage data in the project data/raw/ directory and import the CSV file with read.csv(). Confirm or rename the stage/elevation column to stage. The resulting data frame must contain at least date and stage before it is supplied to rfa_simulate()
stage_ts <- read.csv(
  file.path(project_dir, "data", "raw", "reservoir_stage.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

#Rename the stage-elevation column to `stage` when needed
names(stage_ts)[names(stage_ts) == "stage_ft"] <- "stage"

head(stage_ts)
str(stage_ts)


3.4.4.3 Data Requirements and Checks
Use a stage time series with a consistent observation interval. Daily values are appropriate for typical reservoir stage-frequency applications (such as the included example). If subdaily observations are used, confirm that the selected observation statistic and time of day appropriately represent antecedent reservoir conditions; rfaR samples individual records within each month.
Check that dates can be interpreted as month/day/year values, that stage values are numeric, and that all required months have available stage observations:
# Confirm that date values can be parsed as month/day/year dates
stage_dates <- lubridate::mdy(stage_ts$date)
stopifnot(!any(is.na(stage_dates)))

# Confirm that stage values are numeric and complete
stopifnot(is.numeric(stage_ts$stage))
stopifnot(!any(is.na(stage_ts$stage)))

# Count observations available for each calendar month
stage_month_counts <- table(lubridate::month(stage_dates))
print(stage_month_counts)
Before simulation, compare the available months in the stage record with the months assigned nonzero probability in the flood-seasonality vector. Every month with a nonzero seasonality probability must have one or more corresponding stage observations. Otherwise, rfaR cannot sample an initial stage for simulated floods occurring in that month.
# Identify months with flood probability but no stage observations
months_with_floods <- which(seasonality > 0)
months_with_stage <- as.integer(names(stage_month_counts))
missing_stage_months <- setdiff(months_with_floods, months_with_stage)

if (length(missing_stage_months) > 0) {
  stop(
    "The stage record has no observations for month(s): ",
    paste(missing_stage_months, collapse = ", ")
  )
}

Note: The sampled stage values retain the units and vertical datum of the input stage record. Ensure that the stage record and reservoir model use the same stage units and vertical datum before running rfa_simulate().

title: 7  Function Reference
text:
7.1.1 rfa_simulate()
RFA Stage-Frequency Simulation

Description:

     Performs reservoir stage frequency analysis using Monte Carlo
     simulation to develop stage-frequency relationships. Combines
     stratified flow-frequency sampling, flood seasonality, hydrograph
     scaling, and Modified Puls reservoir routing to estimate annual
     exceedance probabilities of reservoir stage.

Usage:

     rfa_simulate(
       sim_type = "expected",
       bestfit_params,
       dist = "LP3",
       stage_ts,
       seasonality,
       hydrographs,
       resmodel,
       Nbins = 50,
       events_per_bin = 200,
       routing_dt = 1,
       Ncores = NULL,
       sim_name = NULL,
       results_dir = NULL
     )
     
Arguments:

sim_type: Character string specifying the simulation mode. One of
          ‘"median"’, ‘"expected"’, or ‘"full"’. Default is
          ‘"expected"’.

bestfit_params: Data frame or matrix of distribution parameters from
          RMC-BestFit MCMC output. Columns 1-3 are distribution
          parameters:

            * LP3: mean (log), standard deviation (log), skew (log)

            * GEV: location, scale, shape

          Column 4 is log-likelihood (used only in ‘"median"’ mode to
          identify the posterior mode). For ‘"expected"’ mode, must
          have at least ‘Nbins * events_per_bin’ rows. For ‘"full"’
          mode, each row is treated as an independent realization.

    dist: Character string specifying the frequency distribution.
          Either ‘"LP3"’ (Log-Pearson Type III, default) or ‘"GEV"’
          (Generalized Extreme Value).

stage_ts: Data frame of historical reservoir stage with columns ‘date’
          (character in M/D/YYYY format) and ‘stage’ (numeric, feet).

seasonality: Numeric vector of length 12 giving monthly flood
          occurrence probabilities (relative frequencies). Used to
          sample the month of each simulated event, which determines
          the antecedent pool elevation.

hydrographs: List of hydrograph data frames as returned by
          ‘hydrograph_setup’. Each element has columns ‘datetime’,
          ‘hour’, ‘inflow’, and ‘hydrograph_num’, with attributes
          ‘"obs_vol"’ (observed max n-day volume) and ‘"dt"’ (timestep
          in hours). The list must have a ‘"probs"’ attribute
          containing normalized sampling probabilities.

resmodel: Data frame with three columns: elevation (ft), storage
          (acre-ft), and discharge (cfs). Defines the reservoir model
          for Modified Puls routing.

   Nbins: Integer. Number of stratified sampling bins in EV1 space.
          Default is 50.

events_per_bin: Integer. Number of events sampled per bin. Default is
          200. Total simulations per realization = ‘Nbins *
          events_per_bin’.

routing_dt: Numeric. Routing timestep in hours. Passed to
          ‘scale_hydrograph’ to resample hydrographs before routing.
          Supported values are ‘0.25’ (15-min), ‘1’ (1-hour, default),
          ‘6’ (6-hour), and ‘24’ (24-hour).

  Ncores: Integer or ‘NULL’. Number of parallel workers for ‘"full"’
          mode. If ‘NULL’ (default), automatically selects based on
          available cores (capped at 16). Ignored for ‘"median"’ and
          ‘"expected"’ modes.

sim_name: Optional character string to label the simulation. Used in
          the output CSV filename. If ‘NULL’ (default), defaults to
          ‘"sim"’. Spaces are replaced with underscores in the
          filename.

results_dir: Optional path to the directory where results are saved. If
          ‘NULL’ (default), creates an ‘rfaR_results’ folder in the
          current working directory.

Details:

     Three simulation modes are available:

     ‘"median"’ Single realization using the most likely (posterior
          mode) parameter set from RMC-BestFit. Produces one
          stage-frequency curve with no uncertainty bounds. Useful for
          quick screening or debugging.

     ‘"expected"’ Single realization using expected value sampling,
          where each stratified flow sample is paired 1-to-1 with a
          different parameter set from the posterior distribution.
          Produces one stage-frequency curve representing the expected
          (mean) result integrated across parameter uncertainty.

     ‘"full"’ Nested Monte Carlo with full uncertainty quantification.
          The outer loop iterates over all parameter sets (one per row
          of ‘bestfit_params’), and each inner loop independently
          samples natural variability via stratified sampling,
          seasonality, starting pool, and hydrograph shape. Each
          realization produces an independent stage-frequency curve;
          curves are combined on a common stage grid to yield expected,
          median, and 5th/95th percentile confidence bounds. The outer
          loop is parallelized using the ‘future’ framework.

     For all modes, natural variability is captured through stratified
     sampling in with ‘Nbins’ bins and ‘events_per_bin’ events per bin,
     providing reliable coverage from common events down to
     approximately 1e-8 AEP.

     The stratified sampling approach divides the AEP range (default
     0.99 to 1e-8) into equal-width bins in EV1 (Gumbel reduced
     variate) space and samples events uniformly within each bin. This
     ensures adequate representation of rare flood events that would
     require orders of magnitude more samples under crude Monte Carlo
     sampling.

     Post-processing uses the law of total probability via
     ‘stage_frequency_curve’: for a grid of stage thresholds, the
     weighted exceedance fraction is computed within each bin and
     summed across bins.

     In ‘"full"’ mode, each parallel worker independently samples all
     random inputs (seasonality, starting pool, hydrograph shape, and
     stratified z-variates) in addition to using its own parameter set.
     This ensures full Monte Carlo independence across realizations.
     Each worker post-processes its results into a stage-frequency
     curve immediately, returning only the curve rather than the full
     peak stage matrix, keeping memory usage manageable for large
     numbers of realizations.

     Curves from individual realizations are combined by interpolating
     each onto a common stage grid (spanning the global min/max across
     all realizations) in log10(AEP) space, then computing summary
     statistics across realizations at each stage threshold.

     Results are automatically exported as a CSV file named
     ‘{sim_name}_{sim_type}_{MM_DD_YY_HHMM}.csv’ in the ‘results_dir’
     directory. For example, a median simulation named "John McGraw
     Dam" run on June 4, 2025 at 2:30 PM would produce
     ‘John_McGraw_Dam_median_06_04_25_1430.csv’.

Value:

     A list whose contents depend on ‘sim_type’:

     For ‘"median"’ and ‘"expected"’:

     stage_frequency Data frame with columns ‘stage’ and ‘AEP’ from
          ‘stage_frequency_curve’.

     peakStage Matrix of simulated peak stages (‘events_per_bin’ rows
          by ‘Nbins’ columns).

     peakFlow Matrix of simulated peak discharges (same dimensions).

     weights Stratified sampling bin weights.

     For ‘"full"’:

     stage_frequency Data frame with columns ‘stage’, ‘expected’,
          ‘median’, ‘lower_05’, and ‘upper_95’ on a common stage grid.

     all_curves List of per-realization stage-frequency data frames
          (each with ‘stage’ and ‘AEP’ columns).

     aep_matrix Matrix of interpolated AEP values (500 rows by
          ‘Nrealizations’ columns) on the common stage grid.

     common_stage Numeric vector of the common stage grid (length 500).

     Nrealizations Number of parameter set realizations processed.

     Nsims_per_realiz Number of simulations per realization.

See Also:

     ‘flow_frequency_sampler’, ‘flow_frequency_sampler_expected’,
     ‘stratified_sampler’, ‘scale_hydrograph’, ‘mod_puls_routing’,
     ‘stage_frequency_curve’, ‘hydrograph_setup’

Examples:

     ## Not run:
     
     # Not run: Expected and Median modes take ~15s; Full uncert
     # runs ~10,000 parameter realizations and takes 3-4 hours on a
     # typical machine.
     
     # --- Setup ---
     hydros <- hydrograph_setup(jmd_hydro_apr1999, jmd_hydro_jun1965,
                                jmd_hydro_may1955, jmd_hydro_pmf,
                                critical_duration = 2, routing_days = 10)
     
     # --- Expected only (default) ---
     results_exp <- rfa_simulate(
       sim_type       = "expected",
       bestfit_params = jmd_bf_parameter_sets,
       stage_ts       = jmd_wy1980_stage,
       seasonality    = jmd_seasonality$relative_frequency,
       hydrographs    = hydros,
       resmodel       = jmd_resmodel,
       sim_name       = "jmd"
     )
     
     # --- Median only ---
     results_med <- rfa_simulate(
       sim_type       = "median",
       bestfit_params = jmd_bf_parameter_sets,
       stage_ts       = jmd_wy1980_stage,
       seasonality    = jmd_seasonality$relative_frequency,
       hydrographs    = hydros,
       resmodel       = jmd_resmodel,
       sim_name       = "jmd"
     )
     
     # --- Full uncertainty (parallelized) ---
     results_full <- rfa_simulate(
       sim_type       = "full",
       bestfit_params = jmd_bf_parameter_sets,
       stage_ts       = jmd_wy1980_stage,
       seasonality    = jmd_seasonality$relative_frequency,
       hydrographs    = hydros,
       resmodel       = jmd_resmodel,
       Ncores         = 4,
       sim_name       = "jmd"
     )
     ## End(Not run)

title: 7  Function Reference
text:
7.2 Primary RFA Modules

7.2.1 stratified_sampler()
Stratified Sampler

Description:

     Creates stratified bins in standard normal space for use in
     stratified sampling. Stratification improves sampling efficiency
     by ensuring adequate coverage of rare events.

Usage:

     stratified_sampler(
       minAEP = 1e-08,
       maxAEP = 0.99,
       dist = "EV1",
       Nbins = NULL,
       Mevents = NULL,
       verbose = FALSE
     )
     
Arguments:

  minAEP: Minimum annual exceedance probability. Default is ‘1E-8’.

  maxAEP: Maximum annual exceedance probability. Default is ‘0.99’.

    dist: Character. Probability space for stratification.
          Case-insensitive. Default is ‘"EV1"’. Invalid values trigger
          a warning and default to ‘"EV1"’.

          ‘"EV1"’ Extreme Value Type I (Gumbel) space. Recommended for
              flood frequency analysis. Allocates more bins to rare
              events through the transformation ‘-log(-log(1-AEP))’,
              improving tail estimation efficiency.

          ‘"Normal"’ Standard normal (z-score) space. Uniform bins in
              z-space. Use when the underlying phenomenon is normally
              distributed.

          ‘"Uniform"’ Uniform probability space. Equal probability
              width per bin. Generally inefficient for rare event
              estimation.

   Nbins: Number of stratified bins. Default is ‘20’.

 Mevents: Number of events per bin. Default is ‘500’.

 verbose: Logical. If ‘TRUE’, prints a completion message summarizing
          the stratification. Default is ‘FALSE’.

Details:

     The function divides the probability space into bins using the
     specified transformation. EV1 transformation is recommended for
     heavy-tailed distributions common in flood frequency analysis, as
     it naturally allocates more sampling effort to rare events
     critical for dam safety assessments.

Value:

     A list containing:

     normOrd Vector of standard normal ordinates spanning all bins

     Weights Vector of probability weights for each bin

     Zlower Vector of lower bounds for each bin (standard normal)

     Zupper Vector of upper bounds for each bin (standard normal)

     Nbins Number of bins

     Mevents Number of events per bin

Examples:

     # Default stratification
     strat <- stratified_sampler()
     
     # Custom bins and events
     strat <- stratified_sampler(minAEP = 1E-6,
                                 maxAEP = 0.5,
                                 dist = "EV1",
                                 Nbins = 10,
                                 Mevents = 100)
     
     # With verbose message
     strat <- stratified_sampler(verbose = TRUE)
     


7.2.2 flow_frequency_sampler()
Flow Frequency Sampler

Description:

     Generates a stratified matrix of flow values from a single set of
     frequency distribution parameters using stratified Monte Carlo
     sampling. Used internally by ‘rfa_simulate()’ for median-only and
     full uncertainty modes.

Usage:

     flow_frequency_sampler(
       bestfit_params,
       freq_dist = "LP3",
       strat_dist = "ev1",
       Nbin = NULL,
       Mevent = NULL
     )
     
Arguments:

bestfit_params: Numeric vector of length 3 containing distribution
          parameters. For LP3: ‘c(mean_log, sd_log, skew_log)’. For
          GEV: ‘c(location, scale, shape)’.

freq_dist: Character. Distribution type. Either ‘"LP3"’ (default) or
          ‘"GEV"’.

strat_dist: Character. Probability space for stratification bins.
          Passed to ‘stratified_sampler()’. One of ‘"ev1"’ (default),
          ‘"normal"’, or ‘"uniform"’. See ‘stratified_sampler()’ for
          details.

    Nbin: Integer. Number of stratified bins. Default is ‘50’.

  Mevent: Integer. Number of events per bin. Default is ‘200’.

Value:

     A list containing:

     flow Matrix of sampled flow values [Mevent x Nbin]

     nbins Number of stratified bins

     mevents Number of events per bin

     weights Probability weights for each bin from
          ‘stratified_sampler()’

See Also:

     ‘stratified_sampler()’, ‘qp3()’, ‘rfa_simulate()’

Examples:

     # Single parameter set (posterior mode)
     params <- c(4.85, 0.39, -0.15)
     result <- flow_frequency_sampler(params, freq_dist = "LP3",
                                      Nbin = 20, Mevent = 500)
     # Dimensions of result
     dim(result$flow)  # 500 x 20
     
     # Distribution of Sampled Flows
     hist(result$flow)
     


7.2.3 flow_frequency_sampler_expected()
Flow Frequency Sampler (Expected Only)

Description:

     Generates a stratified matrix of flow values by pairing each
     z-ordinate with a different parameter set from the posterior
     distribution. This collapses the nested Monte Carlo structure into
     a single pass, simultaneously sampling natural variability (via
     stratified z-ordinates) and knowledge uncertainty (via varying
     parameters). Used internally by ‘rfa_simulate()’ for expected-only
     mode.

Usage:

     flow_frequency_sampler_expected(
       bestfit_params,
       freq_dist = "LP3",
       strat_dist = "ev1",
       Nbin = NULL,
       Mevent = NULL
     )
     
Arguments:

bestfit_params: Data frame of distribution parameters from RMC-BestFit.
          Must have ‘Nbin * Mevent’ rows (one parameter set per
          z-ordinate). For LP3: columns are mean (log), sd (log), skew
          (log). For GEV: columns are location, scale, shape.

freq_dist: Character. Distribution type. Either ‘"LP3"’ (default) or
          ‘"GEV"’.

strat_dist: Character. Probability space for stratification bins.
          Passed to ‘stratified_sampler()’. One of ‘"ev1"’ (default),
          ‘"normal"’, or ‘"uniform"’. See ‘stratified_sampler()’ for
          details.

    Nbin: Integer. Number of stratified bins. Default is ‘50’.

  Mevent: Integer. Number of events per bin. Default is ‘200’.

Value:

     A list containing:

     flow Matrix of sampled flow values [Mevent x Nbin]

     nbins Number of stratified bins

     mevents Number of events per bin

     weights Probability weights for each bin from
          ‘stratified_sampler()’

See Also:

     ‘stratified_sampler()’, ‘qp3()’, ‘flow_frequency_sampler()’,
     ‘rfa_simulate()’

Examples:

     # Using a pre-loaded parameter set (all 10,000 parameter sets)
     result <- flow_frequency_sampler_expected(jmd_bf_parameter_sets,
                                               Nbin = 20, Mevent = 500)
     dim(result$flow)  # 500 x 20
     
     # Using bootstrapped parameter samples
     jmd_samples <- bootstrap_vfc(
       c(jmd_vfc_parameters$mean_log,
         jmd_vfc_parameters$sd_log,
         jmd_vfc_parameters$skew_log),
       dist = "LP3",
       ERL  = jmd_vfc_parameters$erl)
     
     jmd_result <- flow_frequency_sampler_expected(
       jmd_samples$params,
       freq_dist = "LP3",
       Nbin      = 20,
       Mevent    = 500)
     


7.2.4 hydrograph_setup()
Hydrograph Setup for RFA Simulation

Description:

     Prepares hydrograph data frames copied from RMC-RFA for use in RFA
     simulation. Converts date/time columns and adds sequential hour
     and hydrograph ID columns.

Usage:

     hydrograph_setup(
       ...,
       critical_duration = NULL,
       routing_days = NULL,
       weights = NULL
     )
     
Arguments:

     ...: Data frame representing an input hydrograph with columns:
          Ord, Date, Time, Flow (cfs). Copied directly from RMC-RFA.
          Date & Time should be ‘class() = "character"’

critical_duration: Critical duration in days.

routing_days: Desired length of routing simulation in days.

 weights: Optional numeric vector of sampling weights for each
          hydrograph. Must be the same length as the number of input
          hydrographs. Weights are normalized to probabilities
          internally. If NULL (default), all hydrographs are weighted
          equally.

Value:

     A list of formatted hydrograph data frames, each containing:

     datetime Date-time (POSIXct)

     hour Hours from start of event

     inflow Inflow (cfs)

     hydrograph_num Hydrograph ID number for sampling

     obs_vol Max n-day inflow volume (stored as an attribute of each
          dataframe)

     dt Hydrograph timestep (delta time, dt) in hours (stored as an
          attribute of each dataframe)

     The returned list also has a ‘probs’ attribute containing the
     normalized sampling probabilities derived from ‘weights’.

Examples:

     # Setup with equal weights (default)
     hydros <- hydrograph_setup(jmd_hydro_apr1999,
                                jmd_hydro_jun1965,
                                jmd_hydro_pmf,
                                critical_duration = 2,
                                routing_days = 10)
     
     # Setup with custom weights (PMF 3x more likely to be sampled)
     hydros <- hydrograph_setup(jmd_hydro_apr1999,
                                jmd_hydro_jun1965,
                                jmd_hydro_pmf,
                                critical_duration = 2,
                                routing_days = 10,
                                weights = c(1, 1, 3))
     
     # view normalized probabilities
     attr(hydros, "probs")
     


7.2.5 scale_hydrograph()
Scale Hydrograph

Description:

     Scales inflow hydrograph given a sampled inflow volume from the
     volume-frequency curve. Scale factor is defined by the sampled
     inflow volume and the maximum volume of the corresponding
     duration. If the native hydrograph timestep differs from the
     target routing timestep, resampling is applied prior to scaling:
     finer-to-coarser uses block averaging; coarser-to-finer uses
     linear interpolation.

Usage:

     scale_hydrograph(
       hydrograph_shape,
       observed_volume,
       sampled_volume,
       routing_dt = 1
     )
     
Arguments:

hydrograph_shape: Data frame with two columns: time (hours) and inflow
          (cfs). Must be in that order.

observed_volume: Maximum n-day inflow volume from input hydrograph
          shape.

sampled_volume: Sampled inflow volume from volume-frequency curve.

routing_dt: Target routing timestep in hours. Supported values are
          ‘0.25’ (15-min), ‘1’ (1-hour, default), ‘6’ (6-hour), and
          ‘24’ (24-hour).

Value:

     A data frame with two columns: ‘time_hrs’ and ‘inflow_cfs’, at the
     target routing timestep, with time starting at hour 0.

Examples:

     # Example hydrograph. Requires pre-processing
     hydro_example <- hydrograph_setup(jmd_hydro_jun1965_15min, critical_duration = 2, routing_days = 10)
     hydrograph_shape <- hydro_example[[1]][, 2:3]
     
     # Default 1-hour routing timestep
     scaled <- scale_hydrograph(hydrograph_shape,
                                observed_volume = 50000,
                                sampled_volume = 55000)
     
     # 15-min input hydrograph, 1-hour routing timestep
     scaled <- scale_hydrograph(hydrograph_shape,
                                observed_volume = 50000,
                                sampled_volume = 55000,
                                routing_dt = 1)
     


7.2.6 mod_puls_routing()
Modified Puls Reservoir Routing

Description:

     Performs Modified Puls (level pool) routing of inflow hydrograph
     given a defined reservoir geometry (Stage (ft), Storage (ac-ft),
     Discharge (cfs)).

Usage:

     mod_puls_routing(resmodel_df, inflow_df, initial_elev, full_results = FALSE)
     
Arguments:

resmodel_df: Data frame with three columns: elevation/stage (ft),
          storage (acre-feet), and discharge (cfs). Must be in that
          order.

inflow_df: Data frame with two columns: time (hours) and inflow (cfs).
          Must be in that order.

initial_elev: Starting water surface elevation in feet.

full_results: Logical. If ‘FALSE’ (default), returns only peak stage
          and discharge. If ‘TRUE’, returns the complete routing
          result.

Value:

     If ‘full_results = FALSE’, a named numeric vector with
     ‘peak_stage_ft’ and ‘peak_discharge_cfs’. If ‘full_results =
     TRUE’, a data frame with columns: ‘time_hr’, ‘inflow_cfs’,
     ‘elevation_ft’, ‘storage_acft’, and ‘outflow_cfs’.

References:

     Chow, V.T. (1959). Open-Channel Hydraulics. McGraw-Hill.

Examples:

     # Example hydrograph. Requires pre-processing
     hydro_example <- hydrograph_setup(jmd_hydro_jun1965_15min,
                                        critical_duration = 2,
                                        routing_days = 10)
     hydrograph_shape <- hydro_example[[1]][, 2:3]
     scaled_hydrograph <- scale_hydrograph(hydrograph_shape,
                                           observed_volume = 50000,
                                           sampled_volume = 55000)
     
     # Peak values only
     mod_puls_routing(jmd_resmodel, scaled_hydrograph, initial_elev = 3830)
     
     # Full routing table
     jmd_full_routing <- mod_puls_routing(jmd_resmodel,
                                          scaled_hydrograph,
                                          initial_elev = 3830,
                                          full_results = TRUE)
     head(jmd_full_routing)
     


7.2.7 stage_frequency_curve()
Compute Stage-Frequency Curve

Description:

     Converts a matrix of routed peak stages into a stage-frequency
     curve using the law of total probability across stratified bins.
     For each candidate stage, the conditional exceedance probability
     within each bin is weighted by the bin probability and summed to
     produce the unconditional annual exceedance probability (AEP).

Usage:

     stage_frequency_curve(peakStage, weights, stage_bins = 1000)
     
Arguments:

peakStage: Matrix of peak stages [Mevents x Nbins] from routing.

 weights: Numeric vector of bin weights from ‘stratified_sampler()’.
          Must have length equal to ‘ncol(peakStage)’.

stage_bins: Numeric value of exceedance stages used to compute
          stage-frequency in each bin. Default is 1000.

Value:

     A data frame with columns:

     stage Evaluated stage values

     AEP Annual exceedance probability at each stage

See Also:

     ‘stratified_sampler()’, ‘flow_frequency_sampler()’,
     ‘rfa_simulate()’

title: 7  Function Reference
text:
7.3 Rejection Sampling

7.3.1 pmf_stage_lognormal()
Parameterize a Three-Parameter Lognormal PMF for Stage

Description:

     Computes the parameters of a three-parameter lognormal
     distribution for use as a probabilistic maximum stage (PMF) in
     rejection sampling. The shift parameter defines the lower or upper
     bound of the distribution (typically, the lower value). The
     function supports two modes: (1) supplying a best estimate and
     assuming sigma, or (2) supplying a best estimate, low, and high to
     solve for sigma numerically.

Usage:

     pmf_stage_lognormal(
       pmf_shift,
       pmf_mean,
       pmf_sigma = NULL,
       pmf_low = NULL,
       pmf_high = NULL
     )
     
Arguments:

pmf_shift: Numeric. Assumed lower-bound of the lognormal distribution.
          This will define the shift value. Must be less than all of
          ‘pmf_mean’, ‘pmf_low’, and ‘pmf_high’.

pmf_mean: Numeric. Assumed mean of the shifted PMF stage distribution.

pmf_sigma: Numeric. Assumed standard deviation on the log scale.
          Required if ‘pmf_low’ and ‘pmf_high’ are not supplied.
          Defaults to ‘NULL’. Suggested value = 0.5.

 pmf_low: Numeric. Low estimate of PMF stage (assumed 5th percentile).
          Optional. If supplied, ‘pmf_high’ must also be supplied.

pmf_high: Numeric. High estimate of PMF stage (assumed 95th
          percentile). Optional. If supplied, ‘pmf_low’ must also be
          supplied.

Value:

     A named list with the following elements:

     pmf_shift Hard lower bound of the distribution.

     pmf_mean Assumed mean of shifted PMF stage distribution.

     pmf_sigma Standard deviation on the log scale.

     pmf_mu Derived location parameter on the log scale.

     pmf_p05 5th percentile of the PMF stage distribution.

     pmf_p95 95th percentile of the PMF stage distribution.

Examples:

     # Mode 1: assume sigma
     pmf <- pmf_stage_lognormal(pmf_shift = 239, pmf_mean = 241.9, pmf_sigma = 0.5)
     
     # Mode 2: solve for sigma from low/high estimates
     pmf <- pmf_stage_lognormal(pmf_shift = 239, pmf_mean = 241.9,
                                 pmf_low = 239, pmf_high = 245)
     


7.3.2 rejection_sampling_stage()
Rejection Sampling of Stage Bounded by a Probabilistic Maximum Stage

Description:

     Draws ‘n_samples’ stage values from a stage-frequency curve,
     rejecting any draws that exceed a probabilistic maximum stage
     (PMF) sampled from a three-parameter lognormal distribution.
     Accepted samples are ranked and assigned Weibull plotting
     positions for use in frequency analysis.

Usage:

     rejection_sampling_stage(
       pmf_stage_LN,
       stage_freq_df = NULL,
       aep = NULL,
       stage = NULL,
       n_samples = 1e+07
     )
     
Arguments:

pmf_stage_LN: A named list returned by ‘pmf_stage_lognormal’ containing
          the lognormal PMF parameters.

stage_freq_df: A data frame with AEP in column 1 and stage in column 2.
          Mutually exclusive with ‘aep’ and ‘stage’.

     aep: Numeric vector of annual exceedance probabilities. Must be
          supplied with ‘stage’. Mutually exclusive with
          ‘stage_freq_df’.

   stage: Numeric vector of stages corresponding to ‘aep’. Must be
          supplied with ‘aep’. Mutually exclusive with ‘stage_freq_df’.

n_samples: Integer. Number of samples to draw. Defaults to ‘1e7’.

Value:

     A data frame of thinned accepted samples with columns for z-score
     and stage, suitable for plotting a probabilistically bounded
     stage-frequency curve. Output is produced by ‘thin_samples()’.

See Also:

     ‘pmf_stage_lognormal’

Examples:

     ## Not run:
     
     pmf_ln <- pmf_stage_lognormal(pmf_shift = 239, pmf_mean = 241.9, pmf_sigma = 0.5)
     
     result <- rejection_sampling_stage(
       pmf_stage_LN  = pmf_ln,
       stage_freq_df = my_stage_freq_df,
       n_samples     = 1e7
     )
     ## End(Not run)

title: 7  Function Reference
text:
7.4 Additional Utilities

7.4.1 bootstrap_vfc()
Bootstrap option for VFC (RFA-style w/ ERL)

Description:

     Generates matrix of parameters using posterior mode/mean and ERL

Usage:

     bootstrap_vfc(bestfit_postmode, dist = "LP3", ERL = 150, Nboots = 10000)
     
Arguments:

bestfit_postmode: Vector of distribution parameters from RMC-BestFit.
          For LP3: columns are mean (log), sd (log), skew (log). For
          GEV: columns are location, scale, shape.

    dist: Distribution type. Either ‘"LP3"’ (default) or ‘"GEV"’.

     ERL: psuedo effective record length for bootstrapping

  Nboots: number of bootstraps

Value:

     A list containing:

     params Matrix of bootstrapped parameters

     dist Distribution selected (LP3 or GEV)

     postmode Posterior mode parameters provided to bootstrap

     ERL pseudo effective record length provided to bootstrap

See Also:

     ‘flow_frequency_sampler()’

Examples:

     # Sample using JMD VFC parameters
     jmd_samples <- bootstrap_vfc(c(jmd_vfc_parameters$mean_log,
                                     jmd_vfc_parameters$sd_log,
                                     jmd_vfc_parameters$skew_log),
                                     dist = "LP3",
                                     ERL = jmd_vfc_parameters$erl)
     
     # GEV Example with parent distribution parameters
     gev_example <- c(3.0, 1.0, -0.1)
     gev_samples <- bootstrap_vfc(gev_example,
                                   dist = "GEV",
                                   ERL = 200,
                                   Nboots = 5000)
     hist(gev_samples$params[,1])
     
     # LP3 Example with parent distribution parameters
     lp3_example <- c(3.5, 0.22, 0.1)
     lp3_samples <- bootstrap_vfc(lp3_example,
                                   dist = "LP3",
                                   ERL = 300,
                                   Nboots = 1000)
     hist(lp3_samples$params[,3])
     


7.4.2 qp3()
Pearson Type III Inverse CDF (Quantile Function)

Description:

     Computes quantiles from a Pearson Type III distribution given
     probabilities and distribution parameters (mean, standard
     deviation, skewness).

Usage:

     qp3(p, mu, sigma, gamma)
     
Arguments:

       p: Vector of probabilities (between 0 and 1).

      mu: Mean of the distribution.

   sigma: Standard deviation of the distribution.

   gamma: Skewness coefficient of the distribution.

Details:

     NOTE: This is the non-vectorized version of the function (it will
     be used in a loop) Vectorized version is part of future
     development.

     The Pearson Type III distribution is parameterized by mean (‘mu’),
     standard deviation (‘sigma’), and skewness (‘gamma’). These are
     converted internally to location, scale, and shape parameters.

     When skewness is near zero (‘abs(gamma) < 1E-3’), the normal
     distribution is used as an approximation.

Value:

     Vector of quantiles corresponding to the input probabilities.

Examples:

     # Single quantile
     qp3(0.99, mu = 10, sigma = 2, gamma = 0.5)
     
     # Multiple quantiles
     qp3(c(0.5, 0.9, 0.99), mu = 10, sigma = 2, gamma = 0.5)
     
     # Use with JMD volume-frequency parameters
     qp3(0.99,
         mu = jmd_vfc_parameters$mean_log,
         sigma = jmd_vfc_parameters$sd_log,
         gamma = jmd_vfc_parameters$skew_log)
     


7.4.3 aep2stage()
Interpolate Stage from AEP

Description:

     Given a stage-frequency curve, interpolates stage values at target
     AEPs. Interpolation is performed in standard normal (z-variate)
     space for better behavior across orders of magnitude in AEP.

Usage:

     aep2stage(aep, stage, interp_aep)
     
Arguments:

     aep: Numeric vector of annual exceedance probabilities from the
          known curve.

   stage: Numeric vector of stage values corresponding to ‘aep’.

interp_aep: Numeric vector of target AEPs to interpolate at.

Value:

     Numeric vector of interpolated stage values (same length as
     ‘interp_aep’).

See Also:

     ‘stage2aep’ for the inverse operation.

Examples:

     # Get stage at the 1.12% and 0.175% AEP
     aep2stage(jmd_rfa_expected$AEP, jmd_rfa_expected$Expected, c(0.0112,1.75E-3))
     


7.4.4 stage2aep()
Interpolate AEP from Stage

Description:

     Given a stage-frequency curve, interpolates AEP values at target
     stages. Interpolation is performed in standard normal (z-variate)
     space for better behavior across orders of magnitude in AEP.

Usage:

     stage2aep(aep, stage, interp_stage)
     
Arguments:

     aep: Numeric vector of annual exceedance probabilities from the
          known curve.

   stage: Numeric vector of stage values corresponding to ‘aep’.

interp_stage: Numeric vector of target stage values to interpolate at.

Details:

     Stage-frequency curves typically flatten at very rare AEPs once
     the reservoir reaches the reservoir model discharge capacity. This
     produces tied stage values. ‘approx()’ handles these by averaging
     the corresponding AEPs, which may emit a "collapsing to unique 'x'
     values" warning. This is expected behavior.

Value:

     Numeric vector of interpolated AEP values (same length as
     ‘interp_stage’).

See Also:

     ‘aep2stage’ for the inverse operation.

Examples:

     # Get AEP at stage 3862.0-ft and 3872-ft
     stage2aep(jmd_rfa_expected$AEP, jmd_rfa_expected$Expected, c(3862.0, 3872))
     


7.4.5 interpolate_aep_matrix()
Interpolate AEPs at Target Stages Across Realizations

Description:

     For each realization's stage-frequency curve, interpolates the AEP
     at every target stage value. Interpolation is performed in
     standard normal (z-variate) space.

Usage:

     interpolate_aep_matrix(results_list, target_stages)
     
Arguments:

results_list: List of realization data frames, each with columns
          ‘stage’ and ‘AEP’.

target_stages: Numeric vector of stage values to interpolate at.

Value:

     Matrix of AEP values with rows = target stages and columns =
     realizations.



7.4.6 interpolate_stage_matrix()
Interpolate Stages at Target AEPs Across Realizations

Description:

     For each realization's stage-frequency curve, interpolates the
     stage at every target AEP value. Interpolation is performed in
     standard normal (z-variate) space.

Usage:

     interpolate_stage_matrix(results_list, target_aeps)
     
Arguments:

results_list: List of realization data frames, each with columns
          ‘stage’ and ‘AEP’.

target_aeps: Numeric vector of AEP values to interpolate at.

Value:

     Matrix of stage values with rows = target AEPs and columns =
     realizations.



7.4.7 power_function()
Power Function

Description:

     Raises 10 to the 1st through the nth power

Usage:

     power_function(x)
     
Arguments:

       x: Highest power of 10 to use

Value:

     Vector of 10 raised sequentially from the 1st to the nth power.



7.4.8 theme_rfar_conceptual()
rfaR ggplot2 Theme for Conceptual Plots

Description:

     A custom ‘ggplot2’ theme used in the rfaR conceptual realization
     vignette. Based on ‘theme_bw’ with tightened text sizes, italic
     titles, and the legend suppressed. Intended for figures that
     emphasize curves over annotation density.

Usage:

     theme_rfar_conceptual()
     
Value:

     A ‘ggplot2’ theme object that can be added to a ‘ggplot’ via ‘+’.

See Also:

     ‘theme_bw’

Examples:

     library(ggplot2)
     ggplot(jmd_rfa_expected, aes(x = AEP, y = Expected)) +
       geom_line() +
       scale_x_continuous(transform = c("log10", "reverse")) +
       labs(title = "JMD Expected Stage-Frequency",
            subtitle = "Demonstrating theme_rfar_conceptual()",
            x = "AEP", y = "Stage (ft)") +
       theme_rfar_conceptual()
